stories.headline: Wyoming uranium operation shuts down after cyberattack
stories.claim: Peninsula Energy has halted its Wyoming Lance uranium plant after a cyberattack on its US subsidiary, with no restart date.
stories.summary: Australian uranium producer Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut its Lance uranium operation in Wyoming after a cybersecurity incident hit plant and wellfield control systems. The attack on its US subsidiary Strata Energy was detected on the morning of 20 November, US time. The company says the damage appears confined to operating and control systems, while payroll and corporate systems in the US and Australia are unaffected. It has not set a restart date and cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 guidance of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds of U3O8. The company remains under a voluntary trading suspension until the earlier of 30 November or a restart announcement.

stories.headline: UK to pay 4% 'participation' fee on top of contributions under reset EU deals
stories.claim: The UK will pay the EU a 4% 'participation fee' on top of its main contribution under the reset deals agreed by PM Andy Burnham.
stories.summary: Britain will pay the EU a 4% "participation fee" on top of its operational contribution under the deals agreed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, according to treaty texts published this week. The main payment, made in euros, is scaled to the size of the UK economy relative to the EU, and the fee covers running costs of three EU agencies and systems needed for the food standards and carbon trading agreements. Officials estimate the extra costs at low tens of millions of pounds a year and say economic gains will far outweigh them, though no full total estimate has been published. The deals cover food standards alignment and re-linking to the EU carbon trading regime, and are due to take effect in 2028. A youth visa agreement for 18 to 31 year olds is expected to be published in coming days. Opposition leaders Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage criticised the deals, with Badenoch attacking the government's broad powers to adopt EU law without full votes.

stories.market_take: Mainly a political and fiscal story; the direct cost to the UK is small, though closer EU alignment could matter for UK-exposed trade sectors.

Immigration director Omer Badilla said she was subject to an international alert over links to terrorist acts, a claim that the university's rector's office said it wanted explained. stories.summary: UK architecture studio RSHP has revealed its first project in the Baltic region: Sąvaržėlė, a seven-storey mixed-use office building in central Vilnius, Lithuania. Named after the Lithuanian word for paperclip, the cantilevered, stacked building sits between the UNESCO-listed Old Town and the city's emerging business district. It offers 19,000 square metres of space, including offices, a conference hall, a restaurant and a cafe, arranged around a central glass atrium. RSHP says the ribbed external facades echo the tones of Vilnius's historic architecture, aiming to link the old and new parts of the city.

stories.headline: Christopher Bailey on His Post-Burberry Reinvention at the Historic Burleigh Pottery

stories.summary: Former Burberry creative chief Christopher Bailey has become the owner of Burleigh, the historic Staffordshire pottery, after its parent company Denby entered administration earlier this year. Bailey, who left Burberry in 2018 and was long based in Yorkshire and Oxfordshire, heard about the collapse on a family walk and bought the company in June alongside a small group of private investors. Burleigh's Middleport Pottery site, a Grade II*-listed Victorian factory built in 1888, had been threatened with closure with 62 jobs at risk. Bailey is now focused on digitising the company's archive of more than 25,000 master moulds and engravings. The deal shows a former luxury-fashion executive turning to heritage British manufacturing.

stories.headline: Marketing in the Age of AI
stories.claim: A marketing commentary argues that AI makes decisions harder, not easier, so strategy and brand value matter more.
stories.summary: Marketing has become faster to produce but not faster to decide, the author argues, so the ability to make good strategic choices becomes the foundation of marketing in the AI era. The piece questions whether AI recommendation tools make brands unnecessary, pointing to a CyberAgent survey from August 2026 of 9,278 Japanese people aged 15-69 in which 52.3% said they used generative AI for search, up from 21.3% a year earlier. About 60% of those surveyed said they had bought or used something triggered by an AI recommendation. The author's counterpoint is that AI draws on what is widely discussed, so well-known, consistent brand narratives are the ones most likely to be recommended. Tuition fees for European students remain under negotiation.

stories.claim: Japan's upper house rejected a non-binding censure motion against Education Minister Yoshihiro Seki, 124 votes to 120, letting PM Takaichi keep him in post.
stories.summary: Japan's upper house narrowly voted down a non-binding censure motion against Education Minister Yoshihiro Seki on Friday 27 November, by 124 votes to 120. The motion, filed by seven opposition parties and one parliamentary group, targeted Seki for inviting government officials to political fundraising parties he hosted in 2024, where attendees paid 90,000 yen each, including representatives of biopharmaceutical companies. Seki first told parliament officials attended only two events, then admitted three more had also been attended by officials from the Japan Fair Trade Commission and the Cabinet Office. The result lets Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi keep him in post despite calls for his resignation and gives the government breathing space. Opposition parties had threatened to boycott deliberations on a consumption tax cut bill that Takaichi wants passed before an April start, and the government needs opposition votes in the upper house. The Diet session ends on 12 December, and the scandal could still resurface.

National lost two seats between preliminary and final counts, and the coalition with NZ First and ACT is one seat short of a majority. Opportunity, led by 38-year-old former KPMG consultant Qiulae Wong, won seven seats and 6.1% of the vote and now holds the balance of power. Wong has set non-negotiable conditions on climate action, cost of living and political reform, and has ruled out serving alongside NZ First leader Winston Peters as foreign minister. Luxon, who has run a caretaker government since the vote, previously ruled out working with Opportunity but now says he needs its support. Both Luxon and Labour leader Chris Hipkins have held lengthy meetings with Wong. Officials say forming a government could take weeks or months, and a fresh election is possible if no deal is struck.

stories.headline: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
stories.claim: Trump's new tariff announcement this week is seen as a tentative legal fix rather than a fresh trade shock, with rates due from January or February.
stories.summary: The latest Trump tariff package has arrived with little of the drama of last April's 'Liberation Day', and analysts read it as an effort to shore up the legal basis for the duties rather than a shift in trade policy. The new tariffs are not due to take effect until January or February, the rates are upper ceilings open to negotiation, and the US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has talked of a broad plurilateral talks on excess capacity. The tariffs rest on two legal bases after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency powers earlier this year, and 25 states are challenging the forced labour tariffs in court. China's rate stays at 20% under last year's truce, which expires in mid-January, while Canada faces Section 338 duties that Democrats want to repeal. Economists now expect some of the tariffs to remain for years, and the G20 summit in Miami next month will be a key test.
key_points: The new tariffs are due to start in January or February after a consultation period, and the stated rates are ceilings that remain open to negotiation.

stories.summary: US stocks ended mixed on Wednesday after a sharp early sell-off wiped out more than 1,000 points from the Dow and pushed the Nasdaq down over 4% at one point. The Dow closed up 0.3%, the S&P 500 fell 0.25% and the Nasdaq slipped 0.6%. Nvidia dropped nearly 4%, extending losses from the previous day and giving back part of the gains that followed the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive. Micron fell 4%, Sandisk 5% and Oracle 5%. Anthropic, which listed recently, closed up 1% at about $82.79, just under its $83 IPO price. The volatility follows a selloff last week tied to Huang's earlier resignation and the Anthropic flotation, and it shows how nervous investors remain about AI valuations.
key_points: The Dow closed up 0.3%, the S&P 500 down 0.25% and the Nasdaq down 0.6% on Wednesday.
Early losses were steep: the Dow fell over 1,000 points and the Nasdaq more than 4% before recovering.
Nvidia fell nearly 4%, extending a drop from Tuesday and reversing part of the rally after Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO.
Micron fell 4%, Sandisk 5% and Oracle 5% as the AI selloff spread across chip, memory and software names.
Anthropic closed at about $82.79, slightly below its $83 IPO price, after a weak start to trading.
Investors are still digesting last week's turmoil over Huang's resignation and the Anthropic listing.
stories.market_take: Renewed AI-stock volatility suggests investors remain sensitive to leadership changes and recent listings, so high-beta AI names may stay choppy.

stories.headline: Major East Midlands road projects shelved to divert funding to defence
stories.claim: The UK government has cancelled two East Midlands road schemes, the A38 at Derby and the A46 Newark bypass, to fund defence spending.
stories.summary: The government has scrapped two long-planned East Midlands road upgrades, the A38 roundabouts around Derby and the A46 Newark bypass, freeing up more than £400m for defence. Planned road spending will fall by £428m over the next four years, though the total cost of the two schemes would have exceeded £1bn. The decision followed a June Treasury review that asked departments to cut spending to bolster the UK's defence budget. Regional mayor Claire Ward, a Labour politician, called the move disappointing and short-sighted, arguing that it weakens local infrastructure needed for manufacturing and logistics. Environmental campaigners welcomed the cut, while the Department for Transport says it will still spend nearly £5bn a year on strategic roads and may revisit the schemes.
key_points: The Department for Transport has axed upgrades to roundabouts on the A38 around Derby and the Newark bypass on the A46.

stories.headline: Iranian Foreign Minister Suggests Fatal Drone Strike On Two Italians Is A Set Up
stories.claim: Two Italian technicians from Rheinmetall Italia died in Kuwait after a drone incident; Iran denies involvement and calls it a set-up.
stories.summary: Two Italian technicians working for Rheinmetall Italia have died in Kuwait after falling debris from an incident involving drones that Kuwaiti authorities said were Iranian and that they had tried to intercept. Kuwait's defence ministry said two other workers, one Kuwaiti and one Pakistani, were wounded at a vital site, and Italy's foreign ministry confirmed the deaths at an air-defence surveillance station. Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi rejected any involvement, calling the incident suspicious and a possible 'precooked recipe for war', and offered a joint investigation. Iran's military spokesman blamed the United States and Israel for staging false flags. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed condolences, and the episode raises the risk of wider escalation in the Gulf.

stories.headline: Houthis threaten retaliation over UK military support for Saudi Arabia
stories.claim: Houthis threaten retaliation after UK military support for Saudi Arabia, as Saudi airstrikes hit Yemen's Hodeidah area.
stories.summary: Saudi Arabia has launched airstrikes against Iran-backed Houthi targets in three Yemeni governorates, including the port of Hodeidah, in a sharp escalation of the long-running conflict. The strikes followed a Houthi drone attack on a building in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District that wounded eleven people, and Saudi Arabia says it intercepted several drones near Ras Tanura, a key oil centre. The Houthis have threatened retaliation over UK military support for Riyadh. Yemen's government says its forces halted a Houthi advance toward Aden. The attacks underline the threat to Saudi economic hubs and to its efforts to attract foreign investment, and could affect Red Sea shipping and oil markets.

stories.headline: Taiwan weathers wave of cyberattacks ahead of Saturday's elections
stories.claim: Taiwan faces a wave of cyberattacks targeting officials ahead of Saturday's local elections, with China suspected of interference.
stories.summary: Taiwan has been hit by a barrage of cyberattacks aimed at officials and politicians in the days before its local elections on Saturday 28 November. stories.headline: Two Years After Trump’s Tariff Declaration, Canada Tries to Move On
stories.claim: Canada and the US have moved toward a trade war after talks collapsed, with new 50% US tariffs on about $20bn of Canadian goods.
stories.summary: Trade talks between Canada and the United States collapsed, triggering new 50% US tariffs on about $20bn (C$28bn) of Canadian goods, roughly 5% of imports. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada would retaliate reluctantly, with counter-measures to be released in the coming days, and that the two countries were now in a trade war. The tariffs cover products including wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment, on top of existing US duties on Canadian steel, aluminium, autos and lumber. Trump said Canada wanted the benefits of statehood without being a state. Canada's opposition Conservatives backed Carney. The Bloomberg feed itself gave only a headline, so this summary draws on the BBC report.

stories.headline: EU leaders aim for budget deal before the end of the year, Merz says
stories.claim: Merz says EU leaders will aim for a long-term budget deal this year, with a summit starting 17 December.
stories.summary: EU leaders are aiming to agree the bloc's next long-term budget before the end of 2026, German chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday evening. Leaders will not reconvene for fresh talks on Friday, and a two-day summit starting on 17 December is set to try to close the deal. Merz said a day of Brussels talks had brought "new movement" towards shrinking the proposed size of the budget, a demand made by Germany and other net contributors. He also repeated that all 27 member states should share the cost of aid to Ukraine, an issue still to be resolved. The budget settlement matters for how much the EU spends and how much member states pay in.

stories.headline: Britain’s electricity grid operator makes record number of calls for extra power
stories.claim: UK grid operator Neso issued a record number of calls for extra power as heat and weak renewables strained supply.
stories.summary: Britain's grid operator has made a record number of calls for extra power, driven by colder weather and bottlenecks in moving electricity from Scottish wind farms to consumers in England. The Independent reports that the National Energy System Operator (Neso) issued a rare summer electricity margin notice for Wednesday evening amid a heatwave, then cancelled it after 2pm, saying it was a routine tool and not a sign of risk to supply. An analysis by Kraken found solar covered about half of daytime demand, but the UK had to import around 10% of demand from Europe in the evening as solar faded and several gas plants went offline. Neso paid up to £1,000 per MWh, with costs above £11 million, more than five times the daily average. Batteries helped cover the evening peak.

stories.headline: Saudi Engineer Accused of Bugging OpenAI to Be Released on $1 Million Bond
stories.claim: A Saudi engineer accused of bugging OpenAI's San Francisco office was ordered released on a $1 million bond.
stories.summary: A federal magistrate judge in San Francisco has ordered the release of Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national and US permanent resident accused of planting a listening device inside OpenAI's headquarters, on a $1 million bond. Judge Alex G. Tse said the government lacked enough evidence to keep him in custody, though the ruling could be revisited with more information. Alfozan must wear an ankle monitor, observe a curfew and stay away from OpenAI staff and materials, except for discovery. He was fired and arrested in October, indicted on one count of intercepting oral communications, and pleaded not guilty. If convicted he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The case highlights security concerns at leading AI labs.

stories.headline: Backloggd urges users to change their passwords after a breach
stories.claim: Backloggd, a game-logging site, has disclosed a breach exposing usernames, emails, hashed passwords and IP addresses.
stories.summary: Backloggd, the video game-logging site often compared to Letterboxd for films, has told users to change their passwords after an attacker exploited a bug to reach its admin tools. The site's administrator, MrProg, said in a post dated 25 November that exposed data includes usernames, email addresses, hashed passwords and sign-in IP addresses. Payment details were not affected because payments run through Patreon, and the site does not hold government ID or financial data. The site was taken offline, the attacker was locked out, and all users must log back in. MrProg says game logs, reviews and lists remain intact and that legal advice is being sought before a fuller notice. The site has just reached one million users this month, so the incident touches a sizeable community.
key_points: An attacker exploited a bug to gain access to Backloggd's admin tools, according to administrator MrProg's post dated 25 November.

stories.headline: BoE to cut capital requirements for banks as it warns of AI risks
stories.claim: The Bank of England's Sarah Breeden warned that AI-powered cyberattacks are a systemic risk to banks and the financial system.
stories.summary: Sarah Breeden, the Bank of England's deputy governor, has warned that AI has turned cyber attacks into a systemic risk for the financial system. Speaking at the Institute of International Finance annual meeting in Bangkok, she said banks can no longer assume attackers will not get through and need bare-metal recovery options for core services. The BoE is surveying lenders on their readiness for quantum computing threats to encryption and will use the findings to shape a system-wide response. Her chief worries are hostile states or hackers weaponising advanced AI, and rogue AI agents bypassing safeguards. The headline indicates the central bank plans to cut capital requirements, but the available text covers only the cyber warnings, so the capital move is not detailed here. The source article is dated 26 November, while the reproduced PYMNTS text refers to remarks on 15 October, so the timing is unclear.

stories.headline: UK privacy watchdog faces probe into its workplace culture
stories.claim: An independent review will examine the culture and governance of the UK's data watchdog after John Edwards' resignation.
stories.summary: Britain's privacy regulator is to face an independent review into its culture, governance and accountability, led by Karon Monaghan KC. The review follows the resignation of former Information Commissioner John Edwards in June, after an investigation found a case to answer over his conduct. That inquiry looked only at Edwards, so the new review will examine whether staff could raise concerns and what happened to those who did. It will not reopen the Edwards investigation or examine named individuals. The Information Commission replaced the old ICO on 30 September, and DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy said the government wants to find what needs to change. Monaghan is expected to report in the first quarter of 2027.

stories.headline: Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
stories.claim: Ford has unveiled the GT41, its LMDh hypercar for the 2027 World Endurance Championship, debuting it at a Detroit Lions game.
stories.summary: Ford has revealed the GT41, its new hypercar aimed at winning the 24 Hours of Le Mans again, sixty years after the GT40 took the overall victory. The car was unveiled during the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears football game on 26 November. It uses the LMDh formula, with a carbon chassis from Oreca and standard hybrid parts, while Ford supplies a 5.4-litre V8 derived from the Mustang's Coyote engine and the hybrid control software. Ford will debut the car at Qatar in March, the first of nine World Endurance Championship rounds in 2027, and it is not entering the IMSA series at Daytona. The Hypercar class is highly competitive, with Toyota having won Le Mans and the title this year after three years of Ferrari dominance.

stories.headline: 'Significant number of customer records' pwned in Flight Centre Travel Group breach
stories.claim: Flight Centre Travel Group says a significant number of customer records may have been accessed in a third-party booking system breach.
stories.summary: Australian travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group has disclosed to the ASX that a cyberattack on a third-party accommodation booking system may have exposed a significant number of customer records. The system is used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout and some independent agents. Initial review suggests most records hold only names, with a very small share containing birth dates, emails, limited passport details, phone numbers or, rarely, health or mobility information. The company has contained the attack, rotated keys and is working with supplier and Mandiant, and says flight and corporate bookings are unaffected. The breach follows similar attacks on Booking.com and BWH Hotels, and on RMS Cloud, which led to WhatsApp scams in October.

stories.headline: Rackspace pulls plug on Spot cloud service after security breach

stories.summary: Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers roughly two weeks to move workloads and retrieve data. stories.headline: Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly

Google does not accept PO boxes for developer payment addresses, so many solo developers may have to publish home addresses or pay for a registered agent. Google says the details will be shown worldwide, not only in Europe, which has drawn privacy concerns. Apple is handling the same rules more narrowly, showing addresses only in relevant European countries and accepting PO boxes backed by a bill or receipt.

stories.headline: Google Play will show some app developers’ home addresses to the world
stories.claim: Google will show Play Store developers' contact details, including home addresses for some, to users worldwide from March 2027.
stories.summary: Google will start displaying the contact details of many Google Play developers to users worldwide from 1 March 2027, a move that could expose the home addresses of some solo developers. Developers must declare by 1 February 2027 whether they count as traders under the EU's Digital Services Act. Google treats anyone earning money from apps, through paid downloads, in-app purchases or regular ad revenue, as a trader. For personal accounts the displayed details will be a physical address and phone number taken from the payments profile, and P.O. boxes will not be accepted. The Digital Services Act only requires this disclosure to EU buyers, but Google plans to show it globally, whereas Apple shows trader details only in the EU and allows a documented P.O. box. Developers who do not declare a status risk having updates blocked or apps removed.
key_points: From 1 March 2027, Google will show trader contact details on the Play Store to users worldwide.
Developers must declare trader status under the EU's Digital Services Act by 1 February 2027.
For personal accounts, the displayed details will be a physical address and phone number, with P.O. boxes refused.
The EU rules only require this to be shown to EU buyers; Apple limits its display to the EU and allows documented P.O. boxes.
Developers who fail to declare risk blocked updates or removed apps.
Solo developers earning money in Europe have little room to keep their home address private.

stories.headline: Microsoft: Hackers in China, N Korea using ARTEX AI tool to break into global tech systems
stories.claim: Microsoft says state-linked hackers from China and North Korea are using the open-source AI tool ARTEX in attacks.
stories.summary: Microsoft says Chinese and North Korean state-linked hacking groups are among those using ARTEX, an open-source, AI-powered penetration testing framework, to automate attacks. Campaigns linked to the tool have targeted cloud environments, IT software such as ConnectWise, and financial institutions, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours. Named actors include Salt Typhoon, Crystal Typhoon, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Storm-0940 and Cambodia-based Storm-3358. ARTEX reuses known techniques but automates them at machine speed, and the UK NCSC has warned that such agentic offensive frameworks are fast, cheap and inexpensive to run at scale. The tool was released publicly in July on GitHub, and more than 130 variants are reportedly in circulation. The warnings follow earlier FBI and AWS alerts this month.

stories.headline: China’s Industrial Profits Jump at Fastest Pace in Five Months
stories.claim: China's industrial profits rose 20.1% in October, the fastest pace in five months, led by tech and commodities.
stories.summary: China's industrial profits jumped 20.1% year on year in October, the strongest monthly gain since May, according to National Bureau of Statistics data released on Friday 27 November. Year to date, profits reached 6.737 trillion yuan, up 16%. The rise is driven by high-tech manufacturing, where profits climbed 50.9% over ten months, and electronics, which roughly doubled. Mining rose 38.8% on demand linked to renewable energy and AI infrastructure. Consumer-facing sectors are weak, with furniture profits down 52.4% and auto profits down 26%. Part of the strong growth reflects a low base, since profits grew only 0.6% in 2025. The divergence points to a recovery reliant on upstream and export-oriented industries.

stories.headline: Former OpenAI researcher says the Riemann proof matters less than the fact that an AI system can produce it
stories.claim: Scott Aaronson says AI's maths results, including OpenAI proofs, matter more for what they show about AI than the Riemann hypothesis itself.
stories.summary: Former OpenAI researcher and University of Texas computer scientist Scott Aaronson argues that the real significance of recent AI mathematics results is that AI can now produce such proofs at all. He points to an OpenAI result on matrix multiplication that adds a matching lower bound to an existing fast algorithm, and a faster Fourier transform method that is also proven unable to be much faster. Aaronson says he now feels for the first time that a proof that P is not equal to NP may not be far off. He also says he is virtually certain that AI labs hold one or more major breakthroughs in cryptography, though he has not seen the details. These are his personal views in a blog post, not an announced research result.

stories.headline: MIT’s Robot Builds a Sleeve Around an Arm Without a Stitch
stories.claim: MIT Media Lab robot arm draws a fitted sleeve directly onto a forearm using heated plastic thread.
stories.summary: A robotic arm at the MIT Media Lab can build a sleeve directly around a person's forearm, drawing fine threads of softened plastic until the garment forms in place. The InSituWear project, led by the Critical Matter Group under Behnaz Farahi with research lead Sergio Mutis, skips body scanning, digital pattern-making and seam assembly. The team described the method in an April 2026 paper, showing a sleeve and a glove. A roughly 14-inch sleeve took 22 minutes to make, but durability, comfort over a full day and wrapping flat or recessed areas remain open problems. The approach is an early research step rather than a product, though it hints at custom-fit wearables made with little waste.

Varying strand thickness, spacing and crossing angle lets designers make some areas firmer and others more flexible.

stories.summary: Polish-born designer Daniel Kolodziejczak has turned leftover marble from the yards of Carrara into a new collection, Tesserae, on view at the New York gallery Ateliers Courbet until 16 January 2027. Inspired by ancient Roman mosaics and pottery seen in Pompeii, he hand-carves vessels in marble and pairs them with rock crystal, smoky quartz and citrine quartz. Kolodziejczak, who began as a jewellery designer for Givenchy and Saint Laurent, says he treats furniture like jewellery, aiming for single extraordinary accents rather than room-filling pieces. The exhibition is a good example of how craft and material reuse are reaching the high-end design market.

stories.headline: Supermodel Veruschka, 1960s icon, dies at 87
stories.claim: German-born supermodel Veruschka, a 1960s icon, has died at 87, Bild confirmed on 25 November.
stories.summary: Veruschka, the German-born supermodel known for her shape-shifting presence and body art, has died aged 87, according to Bild, which confirmed the news on 25 November. She died at home surrounded by friends and family. Born Vera von Lehndorff-Steinort in Königsberg in 1939, she was discovered in Florence in 1959 and became one of the first supermodels, appearing on 13 American Vogue covers and on the British Vogue cover in February 1969. She worked with Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, Horst P. Horst and David Bailey, and played a version of herself in Michelangelo Antonioni's 1966 film Blow-Up. Later she turned to art photography with Holger Trülzsch and made occasional runway returns, including for Chanel in 1994 and Giles Deacon in 2011. Her childhood was marked by the Nazi regime, after her father was executed following the 1944 plot against Hitler.

stories.headline: MoD tells 100,000 reservists: be ready for call-up
stories.claim: UK Ministry of Defence has sent letters to about 100,000 reservists and veterans telling them to prepare for possible call-up.
stories.summary: Britain's Ministry of Defence has written to about 100,000 strategic reservists and recently departed veterans, telling them to be ready for a possible call-up, the first such move since the Cold War. The letters, signed by the chiefs of all three armed services, invite volunteers for training such as Nato's Steadfast Defender exercise next spring and ask recipients to update their contact details and skills. The MoD says the aim is to strengthen preparedness and deterrence and improve data on former personnel, and insists mobilisation is not being suggested. The move follows Russian cruise missiles and a drone entering eastern Poland last week, and comes as Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has warned Britain must be ready for war within 1,000 days. The British Army is currently at its smallest size since the Napoleonic Wars, with about 73,000 active personnel.

stories.claim: Oil rose for a second session on Middle East tensions, with Brent near $95 a barrel, while gold dipped and the dollar held steady.

stories.headline: Airline Norse Atlantic says financial situation 'critical,' shares plunge
stories.claim: Norway's Norse Atlantic says its finances are 'critical' and it needs short-term financing; shares plunge 85%.
stories.summary: Norse Atlantic, the Norwegian long-haul budget airline, has said its financial situation is "critical" and that it needs new financing to meet short-term liquidity needs. Its shares closed down 85% on Wednesday, hitting an all-time low and wiping out most of the market value it had left this year. The carrier blamed soaring jet fuel costs linked to the US-Israeli war with Iran and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, and it does not hedge its fuel. It has cut capacity, furloughed crew and suspended unprofitable routes, and it launched a formal sale or merger process in July. It did not say how long it can operate without new money. The squeeze is hitting Europe's weaker carriers hard, with airBaltic in Chapter 11 and EasyJet's sale to Apollo Global Management in train.

stories.headline: Behind France’s Unrest Lies a Historic Decline in Spending Power
stories.claim: Real wage declines and falling spending power are fuelling France's protests, which have spread from schools into wider unrest.
stories.summary: France's protest movement, which began with students in late September, is being fed by a longer-running fall in household spending power. The Wall Street Journal says that as inflation rises, real wages in France are moving in the opposite direction, fuelling demonstrations. Reporting cited from the BBC describes schools blocked, clashes that have injured hundreds, and thousands of arrests, with complaints ranging from staff shortages to the Parcoursup university admissions platform. An OECD comparison, however, suggests the school grievances alone do not fully explain the scale of unrest. The wider picture matters for French politics ahead of the spring elections and for investors watching French public finances.

stories.headline: S&P warns Nvidia's board may be compromised, puts chipmaker's rating on downgrade watch
stories.claim: S&P Global has placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade over governance concerns.
stories.summary: S&P Global Ratings has put Nvidia's AA credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade, citing governance failings after CEO Jensen Huang resigned and was then reinstated within days. S&P said long board tenures may have compromised directors' independence and that governance had not kept pace with Nvidia's growth. The agency could cut the rating within 90 days, most likely by a single notch. Nvidia's shares are down 38% since 6 October, and the stock fell nearly 4% on Wednesday, though the five-year CDS spread was little changed, suggesting limited credit stress. Reports also say the US Justice Department did not formally investigate Huang before the reinstatement, which is a continuing source of scrutiny.

stories.headline: US and Asian stocks swing as AI doubts, Nvidia moves and tariff worries drive markets

Nvidia fell as much as 8% in early trading before finishing 3.4% lower, erasing a brief rebound tied to Jensen Huang's reinstatement as chief executive. Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft also fell, while Meta and SpaceX rose. Earlier in the week Asian shares had rallied sharply on Monday's Nvidia surge, with Taiwan up 9.1% from an eight-month low and MSCI's Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index rising about 4%, but the rally faded as Nvidia slipped on Tuesday. Investors also reacted to Democratic gains in the US midterm elections, which raised fears of tougher AI regulation and data-centre limits. Goldman Sachs expects AI investment above $1 trillion in 2026. US markets close early for Thanksgiving and reopen briefly on Friday.

stories.headline: Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every US child via Trump Accounts
stories.claim: Musk says every US child will receive two SpaceX shares, one from SpaceX and one from him personally, via Trump Accounts.
stories.summary: Elon Musk said on X that every child in the US will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from him personally. SpaceX said on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued Class A share to every currently active Trump Account, and Musk will match that number from his own holding. The pledge doubles the share giveaway Musk promised last month and builds on an October commitment by SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and her husband to give a share to each of more than two million children. Worth almost $18bn at Wednesday's closing price of $127.44, the shares are due to be transferred next month, with Musk's personal share following when his lockup expires in June next year. The White House says almost 70 million Trump accounts have been opened. SpaceX has not said whether the shares will carry a lock-up period or be tied to Trump Accounts, and the move puts private company equity into children's hands, a possible precedent ahead of any SpaceX listing.

SpaceX will contribute one newly issued Class A share to every currently active Trump Account.

stories.summary: Asian share markets staged a strong rebound after a recent selloff, as investors shrugged off fresh US tariff proposals covering 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the EU. Nikkei rose 1.6%, South Korea 1.9% and Taiwan 1.4%, after heavy falls this month of 8% in Japan, 16% in South Korea and 15% in Taiwan. Wall Street also recovered most of its sharp losses before the Thanksgiving holiday. S&P placed Nvidia's credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade over management and board weaknesses. Futures imply a 98% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates by 25 basis points in December, with the 10-year Treasury yield near 4.85%.

stories.headline: Judge blocks FCC early review of Disney's ABC licences, likely violating First Amendment
stories.claim: A federal judge blocked the FCC's early review of Disney's eight ABC station licences, finding it likely violates the First Amendment.
stories.summary: A federal judge in Washington has blocked the Federal Communications Commission from carrying out an early review of licences for eight ABC-owned stations, finding the move likely violates the First Amendment. Judge Loren AliKhan granted Disney and ABC a preliminary injunction and temporary restraining order, and refused the FCC's motion to dismiss the lawsuit. She wrote that the review was no coincidence, noting it began the day after Jimmy Kimmel joked about Melania Trump, and cited eleven occasions on which President Trump urged the FCC to strip ABC's licences. The FCC announced the review in April, even though most of the licences run until 2030 or 2031, and ordered the stations to submit renewals years early. The affected cities include New York, Los Angeles and Chicago. The judge declined to bar all formal or informal FCC pressure, saying ABC had not specified what those might be. The FCC, led by Brendan Carr, says the ruling is wrong and expects to prevail, arguing the review is part of a diversity-hiring inquiry.
key_points: Judge Loren AliKhan granted Disney and ABC a preliminary injunction halting the FCC's early review of eight ABC station licences.

stories.headline: FCC conditionally approves SpaceX plan for up to one million orbital data center satellites
stories.claim: The FCC conditionally approved SpaceX's plan for a constellation of up to one million satellites for orbital data centres.
stories.summary: The US Federal Communications Commission has given SpaceX conditional approval to deploy and operate a constellation of up to one million satellites for an orbital data centre business, a decision taken on Wednesday. The approval is a regulatory win for Elon Musk's plan to move AI computing into space, despite objections from Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society over debris, interference and environmental effects. The FCC set aside some of those concerns as outside its remit, and the order sets conditions on interference with US government systems in the 28.6-29.1 GHz band. It also deferred a decision on SpaceX's request to waive rules on satellite disposal, saying the company had not provided enough detail. SpaceX still needs further approvals, including a debris plan for satellites above 600 km, and has seven years to get its first satellite operational and 14 years to complete the constellation. Technical and funding hurdles, such as cooling chips in orbit and cutting launch costs, remain large, and critics note the economics are unproven.

stories.headline: Bank of Korea raises interest rates amid AI chip boom
stories.claim: Bank of Korea raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point to 2.75%, its first hike since January 2023, citing AI-driven growth.
stories.summary: The Bank of Korea has raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point, from 2.5% to 2.75%, its first increase since January 2023. The central bank said growth was strengthening and that inflation would stay above target for a considerable period, while warning of persistent financial stability risks. The move is fuelled by an AI chip boom: South Korea's economy grew at its fastest pace in nearly six years in the first quarter, and the government raised its 2026 growth forecast to 3%. Consumer prices rose 3.2% in June from a year earlier, partly due to energy costs linked to the Iran war. stories.headline: China places Shanghai party chief Chen Jining under anti-graft investigation
stories.claim: China's anti-graft body has placed Shanghai Communist Party chief Chen Jining, a Politburo member, under investigation for suspected severe violations.
stories.summary: China's anti-corruption watchdog has placed Chen Jining, Shanghai's Communist Party chief and a member of the 24-strong Politburo, under investigation for suspected severe violations of discipline and law, a term that typically means corruption. The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection announced the probe on 24 November, and Xinhua gave no details of the alleged wrongdoing. Chen, 62, had been seen as a strong candidate for the Politburo Standing Committee, making his fall a significant setback. He is the fourth Politburo member investigated since 2025, after He Weidong, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui, extending Xi Jinping's sweeping crackdown that has thinned China's senior leadership and military command. Shanghai's party paper pledged loyalty to Xi and said the anti-corruption campaign would not slow. Analysts say the probe deepens upheaval before the 2027 leadership reshuffle, and investors will watch for any effect on policy continuity in Shanghai, China's financial hub.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump push; investigations and governance questions linger
stories.claim: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on 23 November after Trump pressed for his return; probes and congressional scrutiny continue.
stories.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, president and director with immediate effect on 23 November, less than two weeks after he resigned on 12 November. The board said US government input indicated his return poses no national security risk and that it was satisfied with his candour and ability to lead. Trump said he 'made the deal' by pressing the board, and VP JD Vance reportedly held a private call with Huang and reassured directors. Nvidia shares closed about 31% higher, adding nearly $1tn in market value, and the Nasdaq rose about 6.4%. Huang had stepped down after admitting an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive whom US intelligence has reportedly linked to a Chinese espionage network. Shares then fell 8.5% on Tuesday and remain about 37% below their October peak, and four congressional committees have asked Huang to testify while the SEC, Justice Department and an independent board probe continue. The episode matters because Nvidia is the world's most valuable chipmaker and its governance is now under political and legal scrutiny.
key_points: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, president and director with immediate effect on 23 November.
The board said US government input indicated his return poses no national security risk.
Nvidia shares closed about 31% higher on Monday, adding nearly $1tn in market value, and the Nasdaq rose about 6.4%.
Shares fell about 8.5% on Tuesday and were still down 37% from their early-October peak, according to later reports.
Huang faces questioning before four congressional committees, including a closed-door meeting with three House committees on 1 December, and he will speak at GTC Washington.
The SEC, Department of Justice and an independent board probe into security and IP leakage continue, and Senator Elizabeth Warren has demanded answers.

stories.headline: Kohl’s Returns to Growth in Q3, Raises Outlook
stories.claim: Kohl's returned to sales growth in its third quarter and raised its full-year outlook, sending shares up 19.5%.
stories.summary: Kohl's shares jumped 19.5% to $25.33 after the retailer reported its first sales growth in more than five years and lifted its full-year guidance. Third-quarter net sales rose 1.3% to $3.45 billion, with comparable sales up 1.2%. Net income was $254 million, or $2.15 a diluted share, helped by tax benefits, a real estate gain and tariff refunds; a year earlier it earned $8 million. Full-year net sales are now expected to be flat to up 0.5%, up from a previous decline of 1.5% to flat, with diluted EPS guided to $4.30 to $4.50. CEO Michael Bender credited a turnaround built on clearer value messaging and stronger proprietary brands, though he flagged softness in cold-weather categories.
key_points: Third-quarter net sales rose 1.3% to $3.45 billion, and comparable sales grew 1.2%, the first sales growth in over five years.
Store comparable sales rose 2.0% while digital sales fell 1.0%.
Private-label brands, about a third of revenue, grew comparable sales 3.4%.
Net income of $254 million was boosted by one-off items including tax benefits, a real estate gain and tariff refunds.
Full-year sales guidance was lifted to flat to up 0.5%, with diluted EPS guided to $4.30 to $4.50.
Gross margin rose 1.45 percentage points and inventory fell 1% to $3.9 billion, reducing clearance risk.
stories.market_take: Strong share price reaction to a guidance raise; the stock has a turnaround narrative but is a small-cap retailer.

stories.claim: Prosecutors drop a felony charge against incoming Democratic congresswoman LaKesha Womack over a 2019 rental car.
stories.summary: A felony charge against LaKesha Womack, the Democrat who won North Carolina's 14th District seat in the midterms, has been dropped. Prosecutors had accused her of failing to return a long-term rental car in 2019, a case that was revealed when she was served a criminal summons while campaigning in October. Prosecutors said the vehicle was only returned to the dealer after local police recovered it. The charge was dropped on Tuesday, a week before she was due at a hearing, and she has been attending new-member orientation in Washington. Womack unexpectedly ousted Republican Tim Moore, a former decade-long state House speaker. The reasons for dropping the charge were not detailed in the available reporting.

stories.headline: 300,000 legal immigrants told they’re losing Medicare coverage
stories.claim: About 300,000 legal immigrants are told they will lose Medicare coverage under the new law, with cut-off set for 1 February.
stories.summary: The US Social Security Administration has told around 300,000 legal immigrants they may lose their Medicare coverage, a move that follows changes in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1). Recipients received letters warning coverage may end on 1 February unless they prove they remain eligible. Those affected include older and disabled non-citizens and people with end-stage renal disease, and immigrants who have paid more than $6 billion into the programme. Advocates say the law provides no exceptions and that some citizens could wrongly receive termination notices because of inaccurate records. The agency says it is administering the law passed by Congress and that people can appeal through a hotline or by uploading documents. From February 2027, only four categories of immigrants remain eligible, including refugees and asylum grantees.
key_points: Around 300,000 legal immigrants have been notified their Medicare coverage may end.

stories.claim: Netanyahu demands an end to his corruption trial after judges signal dropping or reconsidering several cases.
stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, still in a caretaker role, has called for his long-running corruption trial to end after judges cast doubt on the charges and recommended dropping or reconsidering several cases. In Case 4000, the most serious bribery case, judges indicated little chance of conviction. The Attorney General said she would consider the recommendations. stories.headline: Lululemon hires Paula Conhain as chief communications officer; SML Group names Jeffrey Fielkow CEO
stories.claim: Lululemon hires Paula Conhain as chief communications officer, and SML Group names Jeffrey Fielkow as its next CEO.
stories.summary: Lululemon has appointed Paula Conhain as chief communications officer, starting 30 November, as the athletic apparel brand works through a turnaround under chief executive Heidi O'Neill. Conhain previously led global corporate communications and public affairs at Ralph Lauren for about four years, and earlier held roles at FleishmanHillard and Gap Inc. She will sit on Lululemon's senior leadership team and report directly to O'Neill, the former Nike executive who is filling key brand and strategy roles. In a separate move, Hong Kong-based apparel label and RFID tag supplier SML Group said Jeffrey Fielkow, former head of the Circular Action Alliance, will become chief executive on 1 January 2027. Fielkow joins the company on 7 December and succeeds Ignatius K.C. Lau, who retires on 31 December after 20 years at the firm, 11 of them as CEO, and will advise in 2027. Fielkow previously ran Tetra Pak units in Vietnam, the US and Canada. The changes are routine leadership moves in the apparel industry, though the Lululemon hire is part of a wider reshuffle as the company tries to reset its image and performance.

stories.headline: Thomas Markle indicted on child sexual abuse material charges
stories.claim: A federal grand jury in Los Angeles has indicted Thomas Markle on two counts of possessing child sexual abuse material, which he denies.
stories.summary: A federal grand jury in Los Angeles has indicted Thomas Markle Sr., the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, on two counts of possessing child sexual abuse material. The indictment doubles the charges from the 6 November federal complaint, which alleged possession of images at two Los Angeles-area storage units and in the Philippines. Federal agents seized about 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books, from storage units he had rented since 2008. Markle has been held in Pinellas County jail in Florida since 10 November, when his release conditions were revoked after he allegedly cut off his ankle monitor, and a judge found him competent to stand trial last week. He denies the allegations, and his lawyer says he vehemently denies the charges. Each count carries up to 20 years in federal prison, and he is expected to be arraigned in Los Angeles in the coming weeks. An indictment is a formal charging step, not a finding of guilt.

stories.headline: US blacklists Singapore-based Megaspeed and Alibaba-linked firms over Nvidia chip diversion
stories.claim: US Commerce Department blacklists Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other Southeast Asian firms over alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China.
stories.summary: The US Commerce Department has added Singapore-based Megaspeed International and six other Southeast Asian firms to its Entity List, a move that requires US licences for any future access to advanced American technology, including Nvidia's top AI GPUs. The listing, announced on Monday 23 November, came the same day Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia chief executive. The department said it suspected Megaspeed of routing Nvidia chips to Chinese companies in breach of export controls, after almost two years of investigation. Three of the listed firms are in Malaysia, one in Thailand and two in Singapore, and applications for licences are likely to be denied. Singapore's prime minister Lawrence Wong said his government is working with Washington on an enforcement mechanism, while noting Singapore lacks full information on chip end users. Malaysia's trade ministry will advise data centre operators not to host or serve the blacklisted firms, though this is advice rather than a ban. China has warned against a technological blockade.

Lukoil's foreign holdings have been under pressure since Western sanctions on Russian oil producers, and Lukoil's shares have been frozen since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The sale would change ownership of significant European diesel supply.

stories.headline: OpenAI pilots Private Inference to shield enterprise prompts from its own access
stories.claim: OpenAI has started testing Private Inference, which keeps business prompts and replies private during processing, with a small group of firms.
stories.summary: OpenAI has started testing Private Inference, a feature that lets business customers run queries on its most powerful models without OpenAI being able to see the underlying data. Chief executive Sam Altman announced the alpha trial on X on Wednesday, saying it is being tested with first enterprise customers. Queries run on sealed-off chips using confidential computing, whose security can be checked independently, and OpenAI says it is securing more compute for a much wider rollout, though it has given no date. Private Inference is the second part of OpenAI's enterprise privacy package, following Private Safety Processing, which began rolling out in September and scans for misuse without storing customer data, keeping flagged content in the customer's own cloud. The move targets the corporate market, where data privacy is a key barrier, and comes as rival Anthropic opened Enterprise Frontier Safeguards to all business users in beta on Monday. Google is pursuing a similar approach with Private AI Compute. Business data is already excluded from training, unlike consumer ChatGPT conversations.

stories.summary: Apple has pulled Talkie, the AI companion chatbot from Chinese firm MiniMax, from App Stores worldwide, citing sexual content, though it did not say whether minors were involved. The removal follows a joint investigation by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and ABC News, which found characters engaging in romantic role-play, verbal abuse and controlling behaviour with minors, including a chatbot that told a 12-year-old girl she would never amount to anything. Talkie, released in 2023 through a Singaporean subsidiary, had about 11 million monthly active users as of October, though its new downloads fell 32.2% that month after tighter age checks. MiniMax, which is Hong Kong-listed, has seen its shares fall about 90 per cent from their March peak, according to reports. The case adds to mounting pressure on AI chatbots over child safety. Separately, 42 US attorneys general challenged Character.AI's plan to auction its platform and user data in bankruptcy.
key_points: Apple removed Talkie from the App Store worldwide, citing sexual content.
Apple did not confirm whether minors were involved in the content.
An investigation by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and ABC News found characters engaging in romantic role-play and verbal abuse with minors.
Talkie had about 11 million monthly active users as of October, and new downloads fell 32.2% that month after tighter age checks.
MiniMax's Hong Kong-listed shares have reportedly fallen about 90 per cent from their March peak.
The case adds to mounting pressure on AI chatbots over child safety.
stories.market_take: MiniMax is not listed in the text provided, so there is no clear listed-stock impact from this removal.

stocks.reason: Loss of a key app distribution channel and reputational damage.

stories.headline: Hawkish Bank of Japan member calls for faster interest rate hikes

stories.summary: A hawkish member of the Bank of Japan's policy board has called for interest rate increases to be brought forward quickly, citing persistent inflation concerns. stories.headline: ESA's Hera probe finds DART left a stadium-sized crater on asteroid Dimorphos
stories.claim: ESA's Hera probe shows NASA's DART impact left a stadium-sized crater on asteroid Dimorphos, which now tumbles in orbit.
stories.summary: The European Space Agency's Hera probe has sent back its first close views of the aftermath of NASA's 2022 DART impact on Dimorphos, the moon of asteroid Didymos. The images show a crater roughly the size of a sports stadium, stretching across nearly the asteroid's entire 151-metre width, and the body now tumbles in its orbit instead of keeping one face toward Didymos. Hera also identified more than 100 boulders in a debris field larger than the team expected. Scientists had predicted a crater of about 20 metres, and the orbit was shortened by 33 minutes and 15 seconds, far beyond NASA's 73-second target, suggesting debris amplified the push. Hera will move from 25-30 km to about 13 km for higher-resolution imaging, and two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, are due to deploy in early 2027 to attempt landings and collect data. The mission is slated to last six months. The results will refine models of how effectively a spacecraft can deflect a dangerous asteroid.
key_points: Hera has revealed a crater roughly the size of a sports stadium on Dimorphos, stretching across the asteroid's full 151-metre width.
Dimorphos now tumbles in its orbit rather than keeping one face toward its partner Didymos.
More than 100 boulders have been identified in a debris field larger than expected.
The orbit was shortened by 33 minutes 15 seconds, far beyond NASA's 73-second target, indicating debris amplified the push.
Hera will move closer to about 13 km, and the CubeSats Juventas and Milani are due to deploy in early 2027.
The findings will help planetary defence planning for future asteroid deflection missions.

stories.headline: Bernard Arnault can lead LVMH family holding company until he is 95
stories.claim: A filing lets Bernard Arnault remain managing partner of family holding Agache SCA until age 95, ahead of a December shareholder vote on a merger.
stories.summary: Bernard Arnault, 77, can remain managing general partner of the family holding Agache SCA until he turns 95, according to a filing this week. The age limit is 18 years beyond his current cap and ten years beyond the age limit for his chairman role at Christian Dior, which is 85. The change is part of a previously announced plan to merge Agache with Christian Dior, which shareholders must approve at a meeting at the end of December. After the merger, almost all of the Arnault family's LVMH stake would sit in one listed entity, Agache. The holding would control 49.76% of LVMH's share capital and 65.55% of voting rights. Legal experts widely describe the partnership limited by shares structure as a 'padlock' on control. Arnault's net worth is estimated at about $130 billion by Bloomberg, and five of his children work inside LVMH.

stories.headline: FedEx jet overruns runway at Miami airport; flights briefly halted
stories.claim: A FedEx cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Wednesday evening, halting departures briefly; no injuries were reported.
stories.summary: A FedEx cargo aircraft overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Wednesday evening, briefly halting flights and leaving only one runway open. Departures were grounded from just after 20:15 local time, and flights were expected to resume around 22:00 local time. The aircraft had flown in from Memphis, and no injuries were reported. The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating the cause. The incident happened the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest US travel days, while heavy rain had triggered flood watches in the area. It follows a nationwide ground stop earlier this month, the longest such halt since 11 September 2001.

stories.headline: Shoe Station Group Dramatically Halts Store Conversions, to Revert Most Locations to Original Banner
stories.claim: Shoe Station Group halts store conversions and will return most of its 131 rebannered stores to their original banners.
stories.summary: Shoe Station Group, the US footwear retailer formerly known as Shoe Carnival, is reversing much of its store rebannering strategy. On its third-quarter call on Tuesday, interim chief executive Cliff Sifford said 104 of the 131 rebannered stores are still under review, with at least 75 per cent expected to revert to the Shoe Carnival name, while 27 Shoe Station at Rogan's stores will return to Rogan's. The company said the upgraded product and higher prices had alienated the Shoe Carnival customer. Returning stores will cost $2 million to $3 million, plus about $4 million in fourth-quarter expenses, mostly falling in fiscal 2027. The move follows a sharp earnings miss and a fall in the share price, and it puts the turnaround strategy under scrutiny.

In-store changes start in early December for the holiday season, with formal banner changes expected in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 because of permits and signage.

stories.headline: Marc Jacobs Sales Hit $509M in Its Last Year Under LVMH

stories.headline: ‘Costly’ Air Freight is Bangladesh Apparel Exporters’ Fallback Option as Orders Slip
stories.claim: Bangladesh garment exporters are paying costly air freight to ship late orders as labour unrest disrupts production and buyers shift orders.
stories.summary: Bangladeshi garment factories are paying steep premiums to fly late orders out of the country, as wage unrest that began in October has pushed foreign buyers to look elsewhere. The BGMEA says factories have already lost an estimated $428 million from production disruptions, a figure it says excludes extra air freight costs, discounts and cancellations. Buyers have moved 59 million pieces of confirmed orders, worth $254 million, to other countries between 1 and 18 November. Air cargo data from WorldACD shows Bangladesh-to-US tonnage up 38 to 44 percent year on year in October and November, while Dhaka's airport remains strained by a cargo station fire last October. The wage board is weighing a demand to lift the minimum wage from 12,500 taka (about $100) to 30,000 taka (about $240), with factory owners eyeing roughly 15 percent. The row matters for global apparel supply chains and for brands sourcing from Bangladesh.
key_points: BGMEA says factories have lost an estimated $428 million, excluding extra air freight, discounts and cancellations.
Buyers have shifted 59 million pieces of confirmed orders worth $254 million to other countries from 1 to 18 November.

Dhaka airport's import backlog reached 400 to 500 metric tons, against over 100 before a fire last October, constraining air capacity.
The government formed a minimum wage board on 1 November; talks were ongoing and about 481 factories were halted on one day.

stories.headline: Abercrombie & Fitch Powers Through Another Strong Quarter, Raises Outlook
stories.claim: Abercrombie & Fitch shares soared nearly 20% after a strong third quarter and a raised 2026 outlook.
stories.summary: Abercrombie & Fitch shares jumped 19.7% on Thursday after the retailer reported a strong third quarter and raised its outlook for 2026. Net sales rose 11% to $1.4 billion, with comparable sales up 6%, and operating income reached $223 million against $155 million a year earlier. Diluted EPS rose to $3.82 from $2.36. The company now expects 6% sales growth for the year, up from 5%, and EPS of $13.70 to $13.90, up from $13.10 to $13.60. CEO Fran Horowitz credited tight inventory control, fewer promotions and growth across brands, and said the Hollister home category test with Target was being evaluated. The 16th consecutive quarter of growth gives the company a strong run into the holiday season.

stories.headline: US Treasury financial crime watchdog hit by suspected cyber attack
stories.claim: US Treasury's FinCEN took systems offline after a cyber incident involving unauthorised access to a limited set of systems.
stories.summary: The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has taken some of its systems offline after detecting unauthorised access to a limited subset of its systems. An agency official said the move was precautionary and that filers unable to submit reports were given temporary relief. The Treasury is working with the FBI, CISA and third-party forensic examiners to establish the scope and impact. A person familiar with the matter said there is no evidence so far of a breach of Bank Secrecy Act or beneficial ownership databases. The incident comes amid a run of technology failures in the US this month, including a nationwide air travel halt and a Microsoft email outage.

stories.headline: US unveils Section 301 tariffs on 14-16 trading partners, with rates up to 20%
stories.claim: The US has announced Section 301 tariffs on 16 trading partners, with duties up to 20%, implementation likely late February or March after a USTR hearing on 25 January.
stories.summary: The US has moved to impose new Section 301 tariffs on at least 14 and, by some accounts, 16 trading partners, including China, the EU, Japan, Vietnam, India and Bangladesh. Duties could reach 20%, according to reporting on the announcement, with rates varying according to the trade deals each country has struck with Trump. The measures stem from a Section 301 investigation launched in March after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's Liberation Day tariffs as illegal. The duties are based on alleged excess manufacturing capacity. China could face another round on top of existing tariffs unless a second trade-truce extension is agreed, and the current pause runs through 10 January 2027. Washington accuses Beijing of falling short on farm purchases and rare earths, while China has extended its suspension of a critical minerals export ban until 27 January. Goldman Sachs estimates the EU at 15%, Vietnam up to 20% or 35% without a deal, and India at 25%. A USTR hearing on 25 January points to implementation around late February or March, and footwear makers warn the costs will fall on American consumers.

The probe was launched in March after the Supreme Court struck down the Liberation Day tariffs.
A USTR hearing on 25 January points to implementation in late February or March, per Goldman Sachs.
Goldman Sachs estimates the EU at 15%, Vietnam up to 20% or 35% without a deal, and India at 25%.
China could face another round of duties unless a second trade-truce extension is agreed.
Footwear industry groups warn the duties will be passed on to American consumers.

stories.headline: H&M: Advancing an Already Mature Business in North America
stories.claim: H&M details North American growth plans, including Puerto Rico expansion and wider rollout of its Move activewear line.
stories.summary: H&M, the Swedish fast-fashion group, says its 26-year-old North American business is mature but still has room to grow, with 478 stores in the US and 89 in Canada. The company opened its third Puerto Rico store in Ponce on 19 November, with a fourth planned at Plaza Las Américas in San Juan for summer 2027, together creating about 65 jobs. Managing director Aneta Pokucinska told WWD that H&M is tailoring ranges to local climates, broadening streetwear and leisure lines, and adding its H&M Move activewear to more than 100 further US stores in December. Over the next year H&M will also donate $100,000 to a Puerto Rican water-resilience nonprofit. The interview shows how the group is trying to grow in a mature market through localisation rather than simply adding stores.

stories.headline: J.B. Hunt Comes Out Against Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern Merger
stories.claim: J.B. Hunt urges US regulators to reject the $85 billion Union Pacific–Norfolk Southern rail merger, joining a growing list of opponents.
stories.summary: J.B. Hunt, the largest US intermodal operator, has asked the Surface Transportation Board to reject the proposed $85 billion merger of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern, arguing it would likely harm shippers more than it helps. The trucking firm, which moves about 2.25 million intermodal loads by rail a year, disputes the railroads' projection of 2.1 million truck-to-rail conversions and says the application does not guarantee benefits will reach customers. Opposition is broadening: CPKC and BNSF have filed critical briefs, BNSF claiming more than 310 errors in the traffic analysis, eight senators and 21 state attorneys general have urged rejection, and the Port of New Orleans has reversed its support. Union Pacific CEO Jim Vena has apologised after a video showed him threatening higher rates for merger opponents. Responses are due in February 2027 and final briefs in May 2027, so a decision is still far off.

stories.headline: Shein’s Europe Sales Sink as New Import Fees Bite
stories.claim: Shein's European revenue fell 27.6% in the latest quarter as EU import fees bite, and its CEO expects pressure to last for several quarters.
stories.summary: Shein's European revenue fell 27.6% to $2.98 billion in the three months to September, as the EU's €3 duty on low-value online parcels, introduced on 1 July, hit its biggest market. Group revenue dropped nearly 6% to $10.27 billion, with the US down 9.4%. CEO Sky Xu said Europe might not recover until the second half of 2027, when most deliveries will come from European warehouses the company is building. A further €2 fee on e-commerce parcels from November could make the year-end shopping season uncertain, and the charge applies per item, so a five-item order could cost €25 in customs fees. Shein's growth outside Europe and the US rose, with revenue from the rest of the world up 18% to $4.2 billion, which now accounts for nearly half of sales.

stories.headline: Higher Fuel Costs Weigh on Apparel Retail Earnings
stories.claim: US apparel and discount retailers report margin pressure from fuel and freight costs tied to the Iran war, with mixed guidance changes.
stories.summary: Higher fuel costs linked to the Iran war are squeezing US apparel and discount retailers, and their latest results show a split picture. Burlington cut its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to $11.70 to $11.80 after taking a $17 million fourth-quarter hit, while Dollar Tree raised its guidance to $8.05 to $8.25. Abercrombie and Kohl's lifted their outlooks, but Gap lowered its own. Diesel averaged $5.95 a gallon from August to October and was $5.695 in late November, still about 49.5% above pre-war levels. Ross Stores is the clearest example: third-quarter sales rose 12% to $6.26 billion, yet its shares fell 2.92% to $213.46 after it guided to a slower holiday quarter. The episode shows how energy costs are feeding through to US consumer retail margins heading into the key holiday season.

Dollar Tree raised its EPS guidance to $8.05 to $8.25, while Abercrombie and Kohl's also lifted outlooks and Gap lowered its own.

Ross guided to 4% to 5% holiday same-store sales growth, down from last year's 9%, and its CFO said higher freight costs were already hitting margins.
Urban Outfitters expects a 75-basis-point fuel-related headwind to persist into early next year.

stories.headline: Too Much, Too Little: Bangladesh’s Wage Hike Pleases No One
stories.claim: Bangladesh's wage board raised the garment minimum wage 36% to 17,000 taka, a hike unions and brands both criticise.
stories.summary: Bangladesh has lifted the monthly minimum wage for garment workers by 36 percent, to 17,000 taka (about $136), after a wage board vote of 4-2. It is the smallest percentage rise for the sector in four decades, and it came after weeks of street protests that had shut 87 factories in Ashulia, Savar and Gazipur. Workers had demanded 30,000 to 32,000 taka, while factory owners had initially offered 15,000 taka. Union leaders called the outcome 'not respectful', while employers argue that direct labour costs of about 42 cents per garment, above rivals in Vietnam and India, leave margins too thin. Brands are being urged to pay higher prices, and rights groups warn that factories could push unpaid overtime to offset the rise. The outcome matters for the world's second-largest apparel exporter and for the buyers sourcing from it.
key_points: The wage board raised the monthly garment minimum from 12,500 taka to 17,000 taka, a 36 percent increase, by a 4-2 vote.
Workers had demanded 30,000 to 32,000 taka, and factory owners had originally offered 15,000 taka.
About 87 factories in Ashulia, Savar and Gazipur remained closed as of Wednesday amid the protests.
Employers say direct labour costs about 42 cents per garment, compared with roughly 31 cents in Vietnam, 36 cents in Pakistan and 38 cents in India.
Rights groups warn that factories may force unpaid overtime and unrealistic targets, and urge brands to share the cost through higher purchase prices.
The next wage revision comes after three years, sooner than the previous five-year cycle.
stories.market_take: Little direct market impact; a modest cost pressure for apparel exporters and the brands that source from Bangladesh.

stories.claim: Cannes mayor David Lisnard, pitching Milei-style spending cuts, surges in French presidential polling and re-elected head of mayors' lobby.
stories.summary: David Lisnard, the right-wing mayor of Cannes, is becoming a surprise force in France's presidential race, polling around 11% in the first round, level with centre-right Édouard Philippe and centre-left Raphaël Glucksmann. He wants to cut €200 billion from public spending, shed 400,000 civil service jobs and shred large parts of labour, environmental and planning law, openly praising Argentina's Javier Milei. On Wednesday he was re-elected president of the Association des maires de France with 72% of the vote, a platform that some mayors say he is using to boost his presidential bid. Rivals call him a 'masked Macronist' or accuse him of plotting a far-right alliance, while he refuses questions on his candidacy. The race is already crowded with Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon leading, so his rise could reshape the centre-right vote.
key_points: Lisnard, 57, is mayor of Cannes and has led the Association des maires de France since 2021, re-elected there on Wednesday with 72% of the vote.
He proposes cutting at least €200 billion in public spending and 400,000 civil service jobs, and eliminating regional health agencies.
POLITICO's Poll of Polls puts him at about 11% in the first round, level with Philippe and Glucksmann.
His New Energy party says membership has passed 150,000.
Critics, including Bardella, call him a 'masked Macronist', while Philippe says voters will reject his libertarian agenda once they know it.
He has not said whether he would back Philippe or Le Pen in a runoff; the French presidential election is still some time away.

stories.headline: Indonesian rescuers resume search for 13 trapped in illegal mine; 13 others confirmed dead
stories.claim: Rescuers resume search for 13 workers trapped in an illegal West Java gold mine, where 13 others are confirmed dead.
stories.summary: Indonesian rescuers are set to resume searching for 13 workers trapped about 100 metres underground in an illegal gold mine in Bogor, West Java, after heavy rain flooded the shaft. Twenty-six men entered the mine on 23 November, and 13 have already been confirmed dead, with six of the bodies identified so far. The search will focus on two shafts using ropes, but narrow, slippery and dark conditions are complicating access, and the search may be paused by bad weather. The disaster highlights the danger of small-scale and illegal mining in remote parts of Indonesia, where regulation is weak. State miner Antam said the mine was not part of its authorised operations. A similar incident at the same site in January killed several miners from carbon monoxide poisoning.

stories.headline: Tusk government ‘facing armageddon’ as European court resumes cases against Poland
stories.claim: European Court of Human Rights resumes about 1,600 cases against Poland over PiS-era judicial reforms, pressuring Tusk.
stories.summary: Europe's top human rights court has restarted proceedings against Poland on about 1,600 cases tied to judicial overhauls made under the former Law and Justice government. The court had frozen the cases in 2023 to give Warsaw time to restore judicial independence, but that suspension expired on Monday. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek estimates compensation payments could exceed €12 million and may grow as judges appointed under the disputed system keep hearing cases. He blamed PiS for the damage and accused President Karol Nawrocki of obstructing repairs, after Nawrocki vetoed a reform bill in February. A second bill on judges appointed under PiS rules has been awaiting the president's signature since 9 November, and Żurek fears another veto.
key_points: The ECHR resumed proceedings on Wednesday against Poland, covering around 1,600 pending cases over 2017 judicial changes.
The court had suspended the cases in 2023; the suspension was extended twice and expired on Monday.

stories.headline: Japan's data centre boom faces growing revolt from urban residents
stories.claim: Japan's data centre boom is facing rising resident opposition in Tokyo and other urban areas, prompting a government review.
stories.summary: Japan's data centre construction boom is running into growing anger from residents, with about 60% of facilities concentrated in and around Tokyo. In Kashiwa, two 31-metre data centres owned by Hong Kong-based PAG loom over homes and send generator fumes into the air. In Tokyo's Koto ward, residents are fighting a planned 51-metre facility by Singapore-based Empyrion Digital, due for completion in 2029, which would bury 1.2 million litres of heavy oil in a flood-prone, high-earthquake-risk area. Residents have appealed to the Tokyo metropolitan assembly for binding rules on noise, heat and fuel safety. The government is reviewing the industry, and an action plan is due by the end of 2026. Consultancy JLL forecasts Japan's data centre market will reach $33.4 billion by 2030, up from $23.4 billion in 2024.
key_points: About 60% of Japan's data centres are in and around the Tokyo metropolitan area, home to about 37 million people.
Residents in Kashiwa and Koto complain of noise, fumes, and safety risks from nearby facilities.
