stories.headline: South Korea minister pushes longer R&D hours to keep pace with China
stories.claim: South Korea's industry minister wants a 52-hour workweek exemption for semiconductor R&D to keep pace with China.
stories.summary: South Korea's Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan has called for semiconductor researchers to be exempted from the country's 52-hour weekly working limit, warning that the industry risks falling behind China. Speaking at a briefing in Sejong on Wednesday 25 November, he said R&D projects that take a year in Korea can be done in three months in China. The proposed exemption would cover researchers earning around 100 million won (about $68,000) a year. Talks are stuck because the Ministry of Employment and Labor wants total working hours capped instead, while the trade ministry wants flexible hours. Kim also pressed for more support for the car industry as Chinese EV makers advance quickly.

stories.headline: “Les COP, c’est une blague” : les critiques enflent contre les sommets climatiques après l’échec à Antalya
stories.claim: UN climate talks in Antalya ended without a high-level deal, the first such failure since 2009, prompting calls to overhaul the COP process.
stories.summary: The UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed without a high-level agreement, the first such failure since 2009. Oil-producing countries, led by Saudi Arabia, blocked efforts to restate the COP28 call to accelerate a shift away from fossil fuels. Critics, including former Obama White House climate adviser Rohan Patel, now argue the COP format should be reformed or scrapped. Germany, France and the Netherlands have published detailed roadmaps to phase out oil, coal and gas, while around 130 countries, including the EU, opposed the text after the fossil fuel reference was dropped. UK climate envoy Rachel Kyte defended rejecting the deal, saying the process could be reshaped. The next summit, COP31, is due in about twelve months.
key_points: Negotiators in Antalya failed to reach a global agreement at the weekend, the first time high-level talks have failed since 2009.

stories.headline: Stalking law simplified to become one offence
stories.claim: England and Wales will create a single standalone stalking offence, but the maximum sentence stays at 10 years.
stories.summary: England and Wales are to create a single standalone stalking offence, replacing the current two, after a review found the law "cluttered and confused". The government has accepted the change, which can be tried in either the Crown Court or magistrates' court. However, ministers rejected the reviewer's proposal to raise the maximum sentence from 10 to 14 years, arguing that the average sentence for the more serious offence was 18.6 months in the year to March. The review was led by Richard Wright KC, and the government has not yet committed to dropping the requirement to prove fear. Victims' families welcomed the report but were disappointed by parts of the response.
key_points: A single stalking offence will replace the two existing offences in England and Wales, triable in either Crown or magistrates' court.

stories.headline: 5 budget battles to watch at the EU summit
stories.claim: EU leaders meet in Brussels on a seven-year budget and a €45bn Ukraine loan, with no deal expected before December.
stories.summary: EU leaders gather in Brussels on Thursday for a summit that diplomats expect will not produce a budget deal on the next seven-year spending plan. Council President António Costa's proposal adds €44 billion in cuts from an earlier plan yet still sits far apart from rival camps: northern states want a smaller, defence-focused budget, while southern and eastern states want more spending on farming and poorer regions. stories.summary: An uncontrolled bushfire on Flinders Island in Tasmania has burned roughly 14,500 hectares, about a tenth of the island, with flames reaching 10 metres. By Thursday midday at least six properties had been damaged or destroyed, and authorities warned that more homes remained at risk. Residents in the north of the island were told to shelter in place as the fire made a significant run towards the south-west, sending smoke hundreds of kilometres south. Six helicopters are fighting the blaze, and crews are building containment lines as conditions improve. Roads are closed, and officials say it is not the island's largest fire but is among the more significant. The Tasmania Fire Service is leading the response for the island's small community.

stories.headline: China launches Shenzhou-24 carrying first foreign astronaut, a Pakistani, to Tiangong
stories.claim: China launched Shenzhou-24 on 25 November carrying Pakistani payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreign national to visit Tiangong.
stories.summary: China launched the Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on 25 November at 8.18am Beijing time, carrying Pakistani pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali to the Tiangong space station. Ali, 40, is the first foreign national to visit the station and the first Pakistani in orbit. He flies with Chinese commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi aboard the spacecraft, which rode a Long March-2F rocket. Ali will serve as a payload specialist and stay for five to 10 days, running more than 90 experiments, including a photosynthetic cyanobacteria study, before returning on Shenzhou-23. He trained for seven months in Beijing, including Chinese-language study and calligraphy. The flight stems from a China-Pakistan space agreement signed in February 2025 and underlines Beijing's push to position Tiangong as an international cooperation hub as the ISS nears retirement around 2030. China aims for a crewed lunar landing by 2030, while NASA targets 2028 for its own Moon landing.

stories.headline: A year after Hong Kong's Wang Fuk Court fire, survivors mourn losses and seek accountability
stories.claim: Survivors of Hong Kong's Wang Fuk Court fire mark one year since the blaze that killed 168 people, still questioning accountability.
stories.summary: Survivors of the Wang Fuk Court estate in Tai Po are marking the first anniversary of the fire that killed 168 people, the deadliest blaze in Hong Kong since 1948, and many say they still feel no justice has been done. Many former residents plan to return to the estate on Thursday to mourn. The blaze tore through seven of the estate's eight 31-storey blocks, which had been wrapped in scaffolding and netting for renovation work. Last month, leader John Lee published an independent report that partly blamed four government departments and accepted the resignation of Housing Secretary Winnie Ho, the first official to step down over the fire. Lee also promised reforms, including laws to criminalise bid rigging in the renovation industry. The government has ruled out rebuilding on the original site and offered a buyback scheme, which most owners have accepted, but survivors such as Yip Ka Kui, whose wife died, say it does little to ease their sense of injustice. Authorities have ruled out commemorative events, though the Chief Secretary says lawful gatherings are permitted and destructive acts will be prosecuted.

stories.headline: Australia and Solomon Islands sign security treaty barring foreign military bases
stories.claim: Australia and the Solomon Islands signed a security treaty in Canberra ruling out any foreign military base on Solomon soil.
stories.summary: Australia and the Solomon Islands signed a sweeping security treaty in Canberra on 25 November 2026, making Australia the island nation's "primary security partner" and ruling out any foreign military or security base on Solomon soil. Prime Minister Matthew Wale attended with 15 ministers, and the signing is widely seen as a counterweight to China's growing footprint in the Pacific. Australia will commit AU$740 million (about US$490 million) over ten years, including AU$670 million in grants and AU$70 million in concessional loans, for education, health, policing and climate resilience. The treaty bars militarisation and foreign interference in sensitive infrastructure such as airports, ports, energy and telecoms, but the clause is not retroactive, so existing Chinese-built assets are not covered. Wale, who took office in May, is trying to unwind close ties with Beijing built under his predecessor Manasseh Sogavare, and says talks with China are ongoing. The 2022 China security pact is still under discussion, and he cannot comment on it due to a non-disclosure clause. The opposition criticised the fast-tracking, and parliament returns in January to approve related reforms.

stories.headline: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves US for Spain, ending 20-month deportation fight
stories.claim: Kilmar Abrego Garcia has left the US for Spain on a commercial flight, ending a roughly 20-month deportation fight.
stories.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man wrongfully deported to El Salvador in March 2025, boarded a commercial flight from Washington Dulles to Madrid on Tuesday night, ending a long legal fight with the US government. The flight was delayed by several hours due to mechanical problems. According to the Washington Post, he agreed to leave under a deal with US authorities that would end removal proceedings, though Maryland court records had not yet reflected such an order. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said he chose Spain over a government flight to Liberia, and suggested he could return to the US later as the husband of a US citizen, possibly after Donald Trump's term ends. The White House and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin called the departure self-deportation and hailed it as a win. Senator Chris Van Hollen, who campaigned for his release, said Abrego Garcia left unharmed and with dignity as a free man. His case followed a sequence of events: he was held in the Cecot prison in El Salvador, returned to face human trafficking charges that were later dropped as politically motivated, and then faced attempts to send him to Uganda, Ghana and Liberia.

stories.headline: Huawei convicted of fraud and trade-secret theft in US trial over Iran business
stories.claim: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud and trade-secret conspiracy, and acquitted it of racketeering.
stories.summary: A Brooklyn federal jury has convicted Chinese telecoms giant Huawei on 10 of 12 criminal counts, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets from American companies. The verdict came on Tuesday, 24 November, after a trial of more than two months with over 60 prosecution witnesses. Jurors acquitted the company of its most serious charge, racketeering conspiracy, and of conspiring to obstruct justice, a result Huawei's lawyer Brian Heberlig called a vindication. Prosecutors said Huawei lied to banks about business in Iran and North Korea and built its business on theft, citing incidents involving T-Mobile, Cisco and Quintel. The case dates to 2018, when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, and to charges announced in 2019. Judge Ann Donnelly will sentence the company on 14 September 2027, with potential penalties running into billions of dollars. Huawei says it fully expects to appeal, and experts say the case has not hurt its business, which has grown in China's AI push.

stories.headline: Dutch court bars BYD Ti7 SUV from EU sales over Land Rover Defender design
stories.claim: A Dutch court banned sales of BYD's Ti7 SUV in the EU over a design-rights ruling in favour of Jaguar Land Rover; BYD plans to appeal.
stories.summary: A Hague district court has banned BYD from selling its Ti7 SUV in the European Union, ruling in summary proceedings that the vehicle infringes Jaguar Land Rover's EU design rights. The ruling was issued on Friday 20 November, and the ban takes effect one week later, also halting production at BYD's planned Szeged factory in Hungary until the case is resolved. The preliminary relief judge found the Ti7, sold in China as the Fangchengbao, was a copy of the Land Rover Defender, which JLR called a 'Defender clone'. BYD strongly disagrees, says the design is its own independent work and plans to appeal, and its shares were reported to have fallen. The ruling is a rare European test of copycat design claims against a Chinese carmaker.

stories.headline: Astronomers may have found a second Earth-like planet on the edge of our Solar System
stories.claim: A paper in MNRAS proposes a hidden 1.5–2 Earth-mass planet, dubbed PX2, at 200–500 AU to explain distant object orbits.

Led by Patryk Sofia Lykawa of the University of South Queensland and Kindai University, the modelling points to a body of roughly 1.5 to 2 Earth masses orbiting at 200 to 500 astronomical units. That is lighter and further out than the roughly ten-Earth-mass Planet Nine proposed by Caltech's Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown about a decade ago. The model reproduces several odd orbits of distant icy bodies, such as the dwarf planet Sedna, though gaps with observations remain. The team suggests the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile could test the idea as it surveys the sky.
key_points: The paper was published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on 23 November.

stories.summary: A single-storey house of about 2,500 square feet has been completed in the Val Luretta, roughly 90 minutes south of Milan, designed by British architect John Pawson. It was commissioned by Noona Smith-Petersen, a Danish-Italian communications manager with a long link to Calvin Klein, and her brother Henrik, who plan one home each on the site. The long, low building follows a single axis, with white plaster walls, pale-grey stone floors sourced from nearby Vicenza, and Danish midcentury furniture including Poul Kjærholm and Hans Wegner pieces. Pawson and Smith-Petersen first met while working on Calvin Klein's Madison Avenue flagship in the 1990s. The piece is a showcase of Pawson's restrained residential style rather than a news event, and is notable mainly for design and architecture readers.
key_points: The house is the first of two planned homes on the site, one for each of the siblings.
Pawson designed it with project architect Giulio Marchesi and it spans around 2,500 square feet on one level.
Interiors use white plaster walls, pale-grey stone from Vicenza, an oak bed and Scandinavian furniture.
Smith-Petersen's husband, Enrico Erba Springorum, is an Armani executive.
The original connection dates to the Calvin Klein store opening in New York.

stories.headline: Genspark built a five-button remote for your AI agents, and it has Cherry mechanical switches
stories.claim: Genspark launches a five-button VoicePad with voice typing, translation and meeting notes for AI workflows, priced with a year of free service.
stories.summary: Palo Alto-based Genspark has unveiled the SecondBrain VoicePad, a palm-sized aluminium gadget weighing 85 grams with five keys and two microphones. Pressing a key dictates text at the cursor, records meetings on the device, or translates speech from more than 50 languages into English. It connects to Mac or PC over Bluetooth or USB-C and is claimed to last around 20 hours per charge. The keys use Cherry MX Ultra Low Profile switches and can be remapped to apps such as ChatGPT or Claude. Genspark includes a year of unlimited voice typing and translation with the device, after which dictation falls back to a free allowance of 4,000 words. The company's 'up to 4x faster' claim rests on speaking at about 160 words a minute against typing at 40. The article is a hands-on style product write-up rather than a major launch, so the device matters mainly to gadget buyers.
key_points: The VoicePad weighs 85 grams and has a CNC-machined aluminium body with five keys.
Keys handle dictation, meeting notes, calendar, slides and the Genspark AI agent, and can be remapped.
Recording happens on the device, with no always-on listening, and 300 minutes of monthly transcription are included.
Output from translation is English only, while more than 50 input languages are supported.
Price was not stated in the text; the company says dictation drops to a free allowance after year one.

stories.headline: The Latest Enamel Pieces by Tiffany & Co. Channel Jean Schlumberger’s Dazzling 1960s Icons
stories.claim: Tiffany & Co. expands its Enamel by Tiffany line with new fall pieces inspired by Jean Schlumberger's 1960s paillonné designs.
stories.summary: Tiffany & Co. is expanding its Enamel by Tiffany collection this autumn with new rings and watches, drawing on the paillonné enamel technique that Jean Schlumberger developed for the house from 1962. The process layers translucent colour over gold or silver leaf and requires several kiln firings. Tiffany recently announced a partnership with the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris to preserve Schlumberger's archives. The Croisillon bracelet, Schlumberger's first paillonné piece, became known as the 'Jackie bangle' after Jackie Kennedy wore it often. The house says it employs some of the few remaining artisans skilled in the method. The story is a luxury jewellery product and heritage update.
key_points: Enamel by Tiffany is being expanded this fall to include rings and watches.
Schlumberger's first paillonné piece, the Croisillon bracelet, debuted in 1962.

Tiffany is said to employ some of the only remaining artisans who can do paillonné.

stories.headline: Dezeen reports from New York's new November design week
stories.claim: Dezeen reports on New York's emerging November design week, as ICFF and BDNY align and collectible design dominates the fairs.
stories.summary: New York is building a second design week in November, with the trade fair ICFF moving in 2027 to run alongside BDNY. The shift raises questions about the future of the May NYCxDesign festival. This year's showings were dominated by collectible, one-off furniture and lighting at fairs including Collectible, Salon Art + Design, BDNY and Basic Space. Dezeen notes strong booths, including Ensemble's installation at Yabu Pushelberg's Tribeca studio and Dudd Haus's milled-aluminium floor lamp. A worker was hospitalised after a light fell at the Collectible fair venue, which the organisers called an isolated incident involving an exhibitor's equipment. The coverage is a design-scene report with some industry context.
key_points: ICFF will run at the same time as BDNY in November 2027, shifting attention away from May.
Collectible moved to a former Upper East Side cinema under development by WSA-linked entities.

stories.headline: Mesaguamo House / Trópico Arquitectura
stories.claim: Trópico Arquitectura has completed Casa Mesaguamo, a patio-based house in Colombia's Cauca River canyon near Támesis.
stories.summary: A house set in the Cauca River canyon of Colombia shows how architecture can frame slow living in a tropical landscape. Casa Mesaguamo, designed by Trópico Arquitectura, sits in the municipality of Támesis, a few hours from Medellín, amid heat and dense vegetation. The architects describe it as a series of patios and living rooms that balance an intimate view of the immediate garden with a contemplation of the distant landscape. The project is presented as a retreat built around the pace of rest rather than speed. It is a residential design story rather than major news, of interest mainly to architecture readers.

The house lies in the Cauca River canyon, a few hours from Medellín.

stories.headline: Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
stories.claim: Dezeen's 20x20 project names Ghanaian architect Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a figure to watch, based on his local practice.
stories.summary: Courage Dzidula Kpodo, a Ghanaian-Scottish... no, a Ghanaian architect who graduated from MIT in 2025, is being championed by Lesley Lokko as one of the most influential architects of the next two decades. Kpodo's MIT thesis became a live site, a five-acre farm in Ghana's eastern region he leased for 99 years in 2022. He buys threatened vernacular laterite buildings, deconstructs them, and reuses the earth blocks to build on his land. His work aims to challenge the idea that Ghana must follow a linear path of urbanisation. The Dezeen 20x20 feature is sponsored by Kohler.
key_points: Lesley Lokko nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo for Dezeen's 20x20 project, sponsored by Kohler.
Kpodo graduated from MIT's master's in architecture in 2025 and won the Arthur Rotch Prize.
His MIT thesis site is a roughly five-acre farm in Ghana's eastern region, leased for 99 years in 2022.
He buys threatened laterite vernacular buildings and reuses the salvaged material on his land.
His work challenges linear urbanisation narratives and seeks to reveal silences in Ghanaian architectural history.

stories.headline: O’Donnell + Tuomey’s Liverpool School of Architecture wins 2026 Building Beauty Awards
stories.claim: O'Donnell + Tuomey's University of Liverpool School of Architecture extension won the overall 2026 Building Beauty Award.
stories.summary: The Liverpool School of Architecture extension by Dublin practice O'Donnell + Tuomey has taken the overall prize at the 2026 Building Beauty Awards. The awards, run by the Royal Fine Art Commission Trust, were presented in London on 23 November. The practice beat three other category winners, with the nearly 3,000 square metre extension built on a former car park beside the 1930s Leverhulme Building by Charles Reilly. The judges praised its interior as the most strikingly Piranesian building in England since Westminster tube station. The practice has been shortlisted five times for the Stirling Prize without winning.

stories.headline: Your First Look at 7th Avenue's First NYC Showroom
stories.claim: Furniture brand 7th Avenue opens its first permanent New York store, a 3,240 sq ft SoHo flagship on Broome Street.
stories.summary: Direct-to-consumer sofa brand 7th Avenue has opened a 3,240-square-foot flagship in a historic cast-iron building at 476 Broome Street in SoHo, its first permanent New York City location and 30th brick-and-mortar space in the US. The brand was founded as a direct-to-consumer business in 2022 by co-founders Billy Shaw (CEO) and Josh Stinson (COO), who say New Yorkers' response to their modular sofas during a earlier pop-up convinced them to put down roots. The showroom uses 14-foot ceilings, a skylight and reclaimed-style details such as coral stone tables and century-old olive oil jars, and encourages visitors to test the sofas, including a 'spill lab' at the opening party. The modular designs, shipped in individual boxes, are pitched to suit small city elevators and narrow pre-war doorways. The store is a lifestyle-led bet on physical retail for a digitally native furniture company.
key_points: 7th Avenue has opened a 3,240 sq ft flagship at 476 Broome Street in SoHo, New York.

stories.headline: Studio Gang completes women's leadership campus in Wisconsin
stories.claim: Studio Gang has completed a women's leadership conference campus on the shore of Geneva Lake, Wisconsin.
stories.summary: Chicago architecture practice Studio Gang has completed the Women's Leadership Center, a conference campus on a lakeside hill overlooking Geneva Lake in Wisconsin, roughly an hour outside Chicago. The project comprises three irregular buildings, the circular Council building, the Lodge and the Cabin, designed to echo the surrounding oak forest through curving volumes and wide windows. It was conceived by former DSC Logistics chief executive Ann Drake, who wanted a place designed around women leaders. Mass timber, low-carbon concrete and white oak felled on the site feature heavily, with a green roof and rainwater collection. Studio Gang recently completed an open-air theatre in upstate New York and a Denver hotel.

stories.headline: Feilden Fowles submits Cambridge college expansion plans
stories.claim: Feilden Fowles has submitted a planning application for a masterplan expanding Cambridge's Hughes Hall.
stories.summary: Architects Feilden Fowles have submitted plans to Cambridge City Council for a masterplan that would expand Hughes Hall, one of the University of Cambridge's postgraduate colleges, by more than a third in student housing. The scheme includes a 116-bed block called Mortimer Villa, a Porters' Lodge arrivals building, and Wileman Court, a study and café building, all in brick and designed to unify a campus the college describes as fragmented. A separate application covers restoring the early 20th-century Covent Garden Hall. The plans rely on low-tech methods, structural timber, natural ventilation, air-source heat pumps and solar panels. The application was submitted in October 2026 and is still awaiting a planning decision.

stories.headline: Have the US midterms brought an end to ‘nasty’ politics?
stories.claim: Analysis suggests US midterm campaigns saw attack ads and anti-trans messaging fall flat, with Democrats gaining from a more conciliatory tone.
stories.summary: Democrats won the 2026 US midterms with a markedly less combative message, and analysts argue that personal attacks and anti-trans messaging failed. Republicans spent at least $274m (about €245m) on ads in the Texas Senate race, yet James Talarico beat Trump-backed Ken Paxton, giving Democrats their first Texas Senate win since 1988. Ohio's Amy Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy after his campaign aired a clip of her estranged mother calling her a liar, an ad a YouGov poll found 64 per cent of voters disapproved of once they knew the background. Analysts say Democrats focused on cost of living and AI and data-centre concerns, while JD Vance has softened his tone ahead of 2028. The piece warns that the mood could shift again before the next presidential race.
key_points: Democrat James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, the first Democratic Senate win there since 1988.
Republicans spent at least $274m (about €245m) on Texas Senate ads without success.

Democrats leaned into cost of living, AI scepticism and authenticity, with some ads saying 'made by humans, not AI'.
Analysts say the tone may not last, and JD Vance has softened his tone ahead of 2028.

stories.headline: Six killed, including children, in plane crash off Mississippi coast
stories.claim: Six people, including three children, died when a small plane crashed in the Gulf of Mexico off Mississippi on Tuesday.
stories.summary: Six members of two families, three of them children, were killed when a Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico off the Mississippi coast. The flight had left New Orleans Lakefront airport bound for Fort Myers, Florida, returning from a fishing trip. Divers recovered the bodies from the fuselage after responders initially found only life jackets, a life raft and the cabin floating on the water. The pilot, Brent Stokes, 50, ran a Fort Myers marine contracting firm. Air traffic control lost contact at about 3:45pm local time after the plane descended rapidly in a turn, and an aviation expert said icing in precipitation could be a factor. Investigators are still working out the cause.
key_points: The Cessna 210 went down between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island in the Gulf of Mexico on Tuesday.
Six people died, including pilot Brent Stokes, 50, his 16-year-old son, and the Knox family: a mother, father and two young sons.
Passengers were returning to Fort Myers, Florida, from a fishing trip that began in New Orleans.

FlightAware data showed a rapid descent in a right-hand turn, and an aviation expert said the aircraft appeared to have serious problems.
Autopsies are under way; the cause of the crash is still under investigation.

stories.headline: Marlboro maker Altria considering takeover bid for Imperial Brands
stories.claim: US tobacco giant Altria is considering a cash takeover bid for Imperial Brands, which would be a major UK takeover.
stories.summary: Shares in Imperial Brands jumped more than 14% to the top of the FTSE 100 after Altria, the maker of Marlboro, said it was considering a possible cash offer for the British tobacco group. Altria also said it was in talks with a third party about buying part of Imperial's business, which could lead to a break-up. Imperial said it had not received any approach, but its board will consider any proposal. Bloomberg had reported that Japan Tobacco was evaluating a bid, and Altria and Japan Tobacco already share a smoke-free joint venture. Under UK takeover rules Altria has until 5pm on 24 December to make a firm offer or walk away. The valuation has risen to about £26bn.

stories.headline: ICE detains man in Massachusetts after he picked up lottery winnings
stories.claim: ICE detained a Massachusetts man days after he won $1 million on a lottery ticket, and Kilmar Abrego Garcia left the US for Spain.
stories.summary: Immigration officials detained Ariel Velasquez-Morales in Massachusetts days after he won $1 million on a scratch-off ticket bought in Boston. ICE said he entered the US illegally from El Salvador in 2013 and was ordered removed in 2014, and it is holding him pending removal. He had taken a lump sum of $650,000, and it is unclear whether he can keep the winnings. ICE publicised the arrest on social media, which drew criticism. The same week, Kilmar Abrego Garcia left the US for Spain, which Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin described as self-deportation. Abrego Garcia said the government did not decide where his story continues.
